source.title: Evaluating Combinatorial Generalization in Variational Autoencoders
source.authors: Alican Bozkurt; Babak Esmaeili; D. Brooks; Jennifer G. Dy; Jan-Willem van de Meent

record.tranche_reason: The study varies VAE network capacity and measures test-set reconstruction performance, bearing conceptually on model-size generalization. It does not reproduce a double-descent experiment or locate an interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The capacity comparisons and their reported test-distortion outcomes are included. Results about changing β and the rate-distortion curves are excluded where they do not measure the effect of model size. The text does not report whether the training set is just fit at any capacity.
record.test_reason: The study varies β (rate strength), VAE depth and width, and train/test split difficulty, and reports test rate and distortion. It never mentions double descent, never locates an interpolation threshold, and compares only 1, 2 or 3 layers (×256/512/1024 units). A fall-rise-fall shape in model size cannot appear or be ruled out with these points. The capacity results are a related construct, the classical overfitting versus overparameterization direction in VAEs. They are recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The capacity statement (helps on easy splits, hurts on hard ones) is in the appendix. The authors' main conclusion is that lowering the rate weight β usually improves generalization. The marginal KL to the Gaussian prior, not the mutual information, drives this. They conclude the standard Gaussian prior is not a helpful inductive bias.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies VAE depth, width, data splits, and rate strength and evaluates rate-distortion/generalization; it does not use a double-descent capacity sweep or identify an interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: Capacity effects differ by train/test split difficulty: the Default split improves with capacity, while the CV (16k/147k) and Checkerboard splits show deterioration in 3-layer architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: At β=1, more VAE capacity improves test generalization on the easy Default split. It sharply worsens it for all 3-layer architectures on the hard CV(16k/147k) and Checkerboard splits (Fig A9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In VAEs, whether added depth helps or hurts test reconstruction depends on the test examples' distance from the training set, not only on model size.

fits_no_version.finding: At β=1 on CV splits, the 1-layer VAE beats the 3-layer VAE for small training sets. The 3-layer VAE overtakes it for larger sets, with a crossover (Fig A12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of overparameterized VAEs appears once training data are dense relative to the test set.

fits_no_version.finding: 1-layer VAEs show a U-shaped test distortion as β decreases on sparse splits. 3-layer VAEs show an L-shape. Early stopping turns the 1-layer U into an L (Fig 3, Fig A17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization-strength curves in VAEs are U-shaped or monotone depending on capacity.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2021), PMLR Volume 130
record.problems: The capacity comparisons use comparatively simple architectures and a limited set of depths and widths. The text does not locate an interpolation threshold or report a full fall-rise-fall test-error curve. Capacity results are described qualitatively in the relevant prose.
record.rows_left_out: No additional capacity-generalization results were left out. Results varying β, early stopping, or training-set size were not extracted because they do not test model-size double descent as defined in V1.

untested.parts: No capacity sweep past an interpolation threshold. Only 1–3 layers and 256–1024 units are compared, and no peak or second descent is sought.
Training-set size is varied (8k–57k), but no interpolation threshold is identified. The double-descent sample-wise question is not posed.

record.verdict_notes: This is a VAE rate-distortion study with no reference to double descent. The reader's V1 'tests' and limits_scope labels are removed because the three-depth comparisons cannot show or rule out a peak near an interpolation threshold. The 'more data' results (CD splits marginally improve with less data) are attributed by the authors to split construction, not to an interpolation effect.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares a limited set of architectures and does not identify an interpolation threshold or test for a peak near that threshold followed by a second descent.
The study evaluates VAEs, not double descent across model classes.

rows.subject: VAEs (architectures with 1, 2, or 3 layers and 256, 512, or 1024 neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Compared network capacities under the standard VAE objective (β=1).
rows.measure: Test-set distortion (reconstruction loss); authors describe generalization as improving with capacity.
rows.value: Increasing model capacity uniformly improves generalization, decreasing both rate and distortion.
rows.locator: Section 4.4, Figure 3; Appendix A3.2, Figure A9
rows.note: The prose reports the direction of the capacity trend, not a fall-rise-fall curve or an interpolation point.
rows.check: Mixes two results. The Section 4.4/Fig 3 sentence is a 1- vs 3-layer comparison across β on CV(82k/82k). The A3.2/Fig A9 statement is the β=1, 9-architecture comparison on the Default split. Three depths with no interpolation threshold cannot show a double-descent peak.

source_check.correct: Appendix A3.2 reports uniformly improving generalization with capacity for nine β=1 architectures on Default. The explicit decrease in both rate and distortion describes the 1-layer versus 3-layer comparison across β on dense CV(82k/82k), with 512 hidden units.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix A3.2, lines 2116–2132; Section 4.4, lines 680–698; Section 4.3, lines 483–485.
source_check.problem: Combines the nine-architecture β=1 result with a stronger rate-and-distortion statement from a two-architecture β sweep.

rows.check: Deterioration at 3 layers on CV(16k/147k) is a monotone capacity effect over three depths. There is no threshold and no larger sizes, so V1's shape cannot be assessed.

relation.reason: Discusses related capacity, overfitting and regularization questions without testing or using double descent; the phenomenon itself is not explicitly mentioned.

tranche.reason: The study examines VAE generalization and rate regularization without establishing an interpolation threshold, a double-descent curve, or another claim version. The reported capacity comparisons cannot determine the claimed fall-rise-fall shape.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv:1911.04594v6, titled Rate-Regularization and Generalization in VAEs, dated March 2021; the pack gives a different title and a 2019 year. No statements or verdict labels are listed for checking.

reader_labels.reason: The direction of the capacity-generalization relationship depends on split difficulty, and the reported comparisons do not establish the claimed peak and second descent; see r1–r6.
